97: Location is the one decision in this plan we cannot fix later, so we choose it before anything else. We look for storefronts with strong foot traffic, a clear view from the street and a neighborhood that mixes offices, a college or hospital, and residents who like to eat out, because a coffee shop with brunch needs weekday regulars as much as weekend crowds. A dining room of roughly 550 to 750 square feet fits {{aforo}} seats between tables and the counter, and the plan assumes about {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day. Outdoor seating is a bonus for a brunch concept, where the look of the place is part of the decision to visit, but it only counts if the lease and the city allow it. We check zoning before we sign anything. Rent and the rest of our occupancy costs come to {{ocupacion_anual}} a year, or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales, and we compare every candidate space against that line, including the lease terms: who pays the building's taxes, insurance and common-area charges, and whether the landlord asks for a personal guarantee.
99: Equipment is the technical core of the business. The two-group espresso machine is the largest single purchase, at {{inv_espresso}}, and it deserves the budget because extraction consistency is what regulars notice first. A professional on-demand grinder, a convection oven for brunch plates and pastries, a refrigerated display case, undercounter refrigeration and a commercial dishwasher complete the kitchen and counter, and the plan carries them alongside the counter and pastry display bar at {{inv_barra}} and the dining room furniture at {{inv_mobiliario}}. The build-out is {{inv_obra}} and the electrical and HVAC work is {{inv_instalaciones}}, which must cover the plumbing the health department expects to see on the plans: handwashing sinks, a three-compartment sink, floor drains and a grease interceptor where the local code requires one. Patio or sidewalk seating adds {{inv_terraza}}. We buy commercial-grade, NSF-listed equipment wherever we can, because inspectors look for it, and we keep a contingency inside the working capital reserve of {{fondo_maniobra}} for items we did not foresee.
101: Supplier choices define the quality guests taste. Our coffee comes from a local roaster that can roast to our profile and deliver often enough that the beans are fresh when they reach the grinder; we agree on delivery frequency, pricing and training support in writing. Pastries and baked goods come from a nearby bakery whose products differ from what the chains sell, or from our own oven if the health permit covers it. Brunch ingredients such as eggs, cheese, avocado and produce need a food distributor or local farms that deliver daily or every other day, and we keep a second supplier for each main category so one missed delivery never changes the menu. Milk is the quiet cost driver of an espresso bar, so we track it every week. In the plan, cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales, built on a food cost of {{food_cost_comida}} and a beverage cost of {{food_cost_bebida}}, with packaging and disposables adding {{consumibles_pct}} of sales. We set par levels, review stock weekly and reorder shelf-stable items on a schedule.
103: We open early on weekdays to catch the commuter and breakfast crowd, and we run the full brunch service on Saturdays and Sundays through the early afternoon. The core crew is the owner-barista, a morning barista, an afternoon barista and server, and a brunch cook, with a weekend extra and relief shifts to cover peaks and days off. The Staffing tab in the workbook shows {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, and it compares the hours we schedule with the hours we need, which gives a coverage of {{cobertura_horas}}. We split the day into opening, midday and close, give each shift a clear lead and use slower afternoons for cleaning, prep and training, so labor follows the pattern of demand instead of sitting idle.
105: A POS system tied to inventory shows what sells, what sits and what runs out, hour by hour. Coffee beans are best used within a few weeks of the roast date, so we order small amounts often rather than stocking up, and we date every bag. Perishable brunch items follow a first-in, first-out routine with a daily expiration check and a temperature log. The POS also handles table orders, takeout and delivery apps, and its sales-by-item report is the tool we use to manage the average check, which the plan sets at {{ticket}} before sales tax. Because card payments are most of our sales, we budget processing fees at {{tarjeta_pct}} of sales, and we set the POS up to collect sales tax correctly for our location and to report it each filing period.
109: A coffee shop with brunch has to be staffed for the way the sector actually works in the United States today: good baristas are hard to find, and they are the first people guests remember. Our model starts with {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, including the owner-manager, who handles supervision, ordering and the books while still working the bar during the first months.
134: The numbers in this plan come from the example case in the Excel workbook and update when you change the green cells. Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}, funded with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a {{prestamo}} loan. We project revenue of {{ventas_a1}} in year 1, {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}} and the pre-tax result is {{resultado_antes_impuestos_a1}}. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} customers a day and cash break-even is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. The lowest debt service coverage ratio over the loan is {{dscr_min}}, and the lowest cash balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, which you can trace on the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab.
112: Opening a coffee shop with brunch takes total startup investment of {{inversion_total}}, of which {{capex}} goes into startup costs and {{fondo_maniobra}} into the working capital reserve, so the cash we need at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. The professional equipment is the core of the spend, led by the two-group espresso machine at {{inv_espresso}}, the item that most defines the quality of the drinks and therefore the value proposition. The build-out is the largest line at {{inv_obra}}, followed by electrical and HVAC work at {{inv_instalaciones}}, and both must meet the health and building codes before we can open.
113: The dining room furniture comes to {{inv_mobiliario}} and the counter and pastry display bar to {{inv_barra}}, the pieces that shape the brunch experience we want to be known for. Patio or sidewalk seating adds {{inv_terraza}}, widening our capacity and making the shop more visible to people walking by. Launch marketing is {{inv_lanzamiento}}, to give the opening visibility, and opening inventory is {{inv_stock}}. We fund the project with {{fondos_propios}} of our own money, or {{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed, and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} nominal interest over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection, so we show it clearly. The working capital reserve covers the first months, before the shop reaches profitability.
115: The plan projects revenue of {{ventas_a1}} in year 1, growing to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3. Year 2 assumes volume growth of {{crecimiento_a2}} and year 3 a further {{crecimiento_a3}}, as the neighborhood adopts the shop, regulars return more often and our routines tighten. The model has two clearly different revenue lines: beverages, with a cost of {{food_cost_bebida}} of beverage sales, and brunch and food, with a cost of {{food_cost_comida}} of food sales. Together they give a cost of goods of {{cogs_pct}} and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}, which has to absorb labor, rent, utilities and overhead. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, and net profit rises from {{resultado_neto_a1}} to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}} over the three years.
116: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} customers a day at an average check of {{ticket}}, or {{equilibrio_ventas}} of revenue a year. That figure weighs our fixed costs, including rent, payroll, utilities and depreciation of {{amortizacion_anual}}, against the contribution of each sale. Cash break-even (loan payments in, depreciation out) is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} customers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}} a year, so our margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}. Our year-1 plan is {{clientes_dia}} customers a day over {{dias}} opening days, which averages {{ventas_dia}} in sales per opening day.
118: The workbook tests three scenarios to show how sensitive the project is to demand. In the pessimistic case we serve {{pesimista_clientes}} customers a day, revenue is {{pesimista_ventas}} and the pre-tax result is {{pesimista_resultado}}. In the optimistic case we serve {{optimista_clientes}} customers a day, revenue is {{optimista_ventas}} and the pre-tax result is {{optimista_resultado}}. The base case is the one described above, and it is the number we ask the bank to underwrite. Seeing all three side by side tells us how much room we have if weekday traffic builds more slowly than we expect.
119: Project payback before debt is {{payback}}, and payback on startup costs alone is {{payback_capex}}. Recovering capital over several years is normal in food service, because a new shop needs time to build regulars and to learn its own seasonality. For the lender, the key figure is the debt service coverage ratio: the lowest value over the loan is {{dscr_min}}, compared with the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for, and the workbook uses {{dscr_limite}} as its own warning limit. The lowest year-1 cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}}. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed and your own results will depend on your costs and your location.
121: The lead barista has to meet standards that the market now expects: command of espresso extraction and dialing in, intermediate-to-advanced latte art, knowledge of origins and cup profiles, and hands-on experience maintaining espresso equipment. This person is the most valuable asset in the project, responsible for the consistency of every drink and for training the rest of the team. In a specialty shop, the barista at the bar is the brand, so we hire for craft and for hospitality, and we pay accordingly.
122: The barista-servers combine basic drink preparation with guest service and need to handle plant-based milks, quick breakfasts and our service routines. The brunch cook needs experience with plates such as eggs Benedict, avocado toast and pancakes, plus baked goods, and must understand allergen rules and the HACCP-based food safety plan.
124: In year 1, our labor cost is {{personal_a1}} including employer payroll taxes, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. We estimate payroll taxes at {{cargas_pct}} of wages, which covers the employer share of Social Security and Medicare, federal and state unemployment taxes and workers' compensation insurance; your actual rate depends on your state and insurer. Employees are hired on a W-2 and paid through payroll. Every wage has to clear the legal floor: the federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, about {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time position of {{horas_semana}} hours a week, and many states and cities set a higher minimum that applies instead.
125: The Staffing tab sets the monthly pay of each role in the example: the owner-barista, a morning barista, an afternoon barista and server, a brunch cook, a weekend extra and relief shifts. Replace those figures with the going rates in your market, and make sure none falls below your state or local minimum. The workbook does not model tips, which vary widely and are treated under separate payroll tax rules, so treat them as extra income for the team rather than as a reason to pay less. The owner-manager can take a modest salary at first and draw more from profits once the shop is established.
127: Shifts follow the demand pattern of a coffee shop with brunch. Weekday mornings peak for commuters and quick breakfasts and then ease off through the afternoon, while weekend brunch brings the busiest hours of the week from late morning through mid-afternoon. A typical weekday morning team is the lead barista and a barista-server, and on weekends we add the brunch cook and the weekend extra. We publish schedules in advance, with clear handoffs between shifts, and we review sales by hour each month to move hours to where the guests are.
128: Full-time schedules are 40 hours a week over five days, which keeps most roles under the point where federal overtime pay begins for non-exempt employees, and we keep time and payroll records for every employee, as the Fair Labor Standards Act requires. We stay flexible about seasonality and local events. The owner works the operation directly for the first six months and then moves toward supervision and administration once the team is settled.
130: The training plan front-loads the first month of operation. It covers standardized espresso extraction following Specialty Coffee Association guidelines, quality control for milk drinks, the brunch menu with detailed recipe cards, and allergen handling: federal law recognizes nine major food allergens, and we train everyone to answer questions and prevent cross-contact. Everyone who handles food gets a food handler card where the state or county requires one, and at least one Certified Food Protection Manager, for example through ServSafe, is on the team. We add service standards and a clear way to handle complaints.
131: Ongoing training takes the form of short weekly quality meetings and a monthly session to develop new recipes and seasonal drinks. This investment in people is decisive in a market where the guest experience depends directly on the skill of the barista team, and it is also how we keep good people from leaving.
137: Choosing the legal structure is the first administrative step, and it determines liability and taxes. For a coffee shop like this one, most owners choose either a sole proprietorship or a limited liability company. The U.S. Small Business Administration notes that you are automatically a sole proprietorship if you do business without registering as anything else, and that an LLC generally protects your personal assets, such as your home and savings, from business liabilities. An LLC is registered with the state, usually through the Secretary of State's office, and most states expect a registered agent and an operating agreement. We also obtain an Employer Identification Number from the IRS; applying is free, and it is needed to hire employees and to pay sales and excise taxes. Talk to an accountant or an attorney about which structure fits your situation.
138: Next come the tax and business registrations. Most shops need a business license from the city or county and a registration with the state tax agency, often called a seller's permit or sales tax permit, so the business can collect sales tax on food and drinks. If we trade under a name different from the legal name, we register a DBA, also known as a trade name or assumed name, with the state, county or city as required. The SBA's licensing guide explains that requirements depend on the business activity and location at the federal, state and local levels, so we confirm each item with the local office before spending money. We also set up payroll and withholding accounts with the state before the first hire.
139: Before signing a lease, we confirm with the city that the zoning allows a food service use at that address, because zoning rules can restrict or ban some kinds of businesses in an area. A build-out normally needs building permits for the construction, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work, and the city issues a certificate of occupancy once the space passes its final inspections; some cities also ask for approval from the fire department. Renovating a former restaurant can be faster than converting a retail shell, but only if the existing permits and the grease interceptor still meet the current code. Timelines vary a great deal from one city to the next, so we put these steps first on the schedule and build in a cushion before the opening date.
140: A coffee shop that serves food needs a food establishment health permit from the local health department. The usual process is a plan review of the layout, equipment and menu before construction, followed by an inspection before opening, so we submit the plans early. Health codes are based on the FDA Food Code, which each state adopts in its own way. In most places we need at least one Certified Food Protection Manager and food handler cards for the rest of the staff where required, and some jurisdictions ask for a written HACCP-based food safety plan for certain practices. Allergens are the main control point of a brunch menu: federal law recognizes nine major allergens, which are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame, and we keep plant-based milks and ingredients such as almond and soy clearly labeled and separate to prevent cross-contact.
141: Several smaller permits matter for this concept. A sidewalk café or outdoor seating permit is usually issued by the city, often for a set season, and may require insurance and a layout showing clear walkways; we apply well before opening, because the patio is part of the brunch experience. Exterior signs normally need a sign permit and must comply with zoning and landlord rules. We hold a liquor license only if we choose to serve alcohol, such as mimosas or beer with brunch; state alcohol agencies set their own rules, the process can take months, and the license is never needed for a coffee-only menu. If we play music in the shop, we check whether licenses from ASCAP, BMI or SESAC are needed.
142: As an employer, we follow federal and state rules from the first hire: Form I-9 to verify work eligibility, Form W-4 for withholding, state new-hire reporting, workers' compensation insurance (required in almost every state) and the basic safety practices that OSHA expects, including training and a safe kitchen. For insurance we plan on general liability coverage, which landlords and many cities require, and a business owner's policy covering property and equipment. Putting these steps into the plan from the start prevents delays at opening and avoids fines. A note for readers in the United Kingdom: register the food business with the local council at least 28 days before trading, which is free, and ask the council about permission for tables on the street. Expect a hygiene inspection and a Food Hygiene Rating from 1 to 5, VAT at 20% on hot food and on food eaten on the premises, and 14 declared allergens.
145: The market is moving our way. Specialty coffee has spread from big-city neighborhoods to suburbs and smaller cities, and brunch has become a fixed weekend occasion, so a well-run neighborhood shop that does both meets demand that in many places still outruns supply. Brunch also lifts the check: a guest who adds a plate to a drink spends more than one who orders coffee and a pastry. We build our numbers bottom-up, from {{clientes_dia}} customers a day, an average check of {{ticket}} and {{dias}} opening days a year, rather than leaning on a national growth figure. Combining quality coffee with weekend brunch answers a lasting change in how people choose where to eat out, not a passing trend, and the opportunity rests on our own numbers.
146: The risks exist and we name them honestly. Brunch concentrates demand on weekends, so the shop still has to earn its keep from Monday to Friday with coffee and breakfast, and a location with weak weekday traffic erodes the whole model. Seasonality hits some locations harder, especially tourist areas and cold climates where the patio cannot be used year-round. Location is the first risk to rule out before committing capital, and we validate it with our own traffic counts at different hours. Finally, coffee is a high-margin product with limited volume, so covering fixed costs for the space, the team and depreciation takes sustained daily volume: our accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} customers a day and the plan assumes {{clientes_dia}}.
147: Our main strength is a controlled investment. Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}, a fraction of what a full-service restaurant requires, and the plan funds it with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a {{prestamo}} loan. Beverages carry a cost of only {{food_cost_bebida}} of beverage sales, which leaves room to pay for labor and rent when quality control is tight and the team is trained in extraction. Loyalty works in our favor: a guest who buys quality coffee several times a week is worth far more over a year than any single visit suggests. A photogenic room, a patio and a consistent look act as free marketing when combined with an active review and social media strategy.
148: Execution has to follow a precise timeline, and it mirrors the phases of the opening checklist included with this kit. In Phase 1 - Business Setup we form the company, obtain an EIN, register for taxes, open a business bank account and secure insurance. In Phase 2 - Location & Permits we validate the location with real traffic counts, review the lease, check zoning, and start the plan review and building permits. In Phase 3 - Build-Out & Equipment we carry out the construction, install the two-group espresso machine and the kitchen equipment, and pass the final inspections to obtain the certificate of occupancy. In Phase 4 - Staff we hire the lead barista and the crew and train them on espresso, latte art, the brunch menu and allergens. In Phase 5 - Marketing we set up our Google Business Profile, Yelp and social profiles and the launch campaign. In Phase 6 - First 90 Days we run a soft opening with reduced hours, collect feedback actively and adjust before the full launch.
149: We track key performance indicators every week from day one. Our target is {{clientes_dia}} customers a day, and the average check, planned at {{ticket}}, tells us whether brunch add-ons are working. Sales per opening day, planned at {{ventas_dia}}, show how well the shop is performing against the plan. Cost of goods against the planned {{cogs_pct}} and labor against {{personal_pct}} of sales tell us early if margins are slipping, and we control portions and waste to hold them. We also watch new Google and Yelp reviews each month and the rate of returning customers as signs of satisfaction and word of mouth.
150: Looking three years ahead, the shop should generate enough cash to fund a second location in another neighborhood or to build a retail line of our own roasted coffee for sale to consumers and other cafes. Our vision for this kind of project is clear: demonstrable profitability in year 1, scalability in year 2 and diversified revenue in year 3. The model works when it is executed with rigor in the choice of location, the training of the team and discipline in operating costs. Replace the example numbers in the workbook with your own, review the legal checklist with your local authorities and your accountant, and bring the plan to the bank with confidence.
